title: Interview prep sheet: STAR stories for a maintenance tech role (example candidate)
summary: Fictional candidate Maya Ortega's STAR stories for a maintenance tech interview — situations you can adapt, not a biography.

blocks.title: STAR stories you can rehearse aloud
blocks.body: Maya Ortega is a fictional maintenance tech preparing for a plant interview. The stories below are invented examples in STAR form — Situation, Task, Action, Result — so you can practice structure without borrowing anyone's real resume.

blocks.title: All people and plants here are fictional
blocks.body: Names, employers, and metrics are made up for rehearsal. Swap in your own verified stories before any real interview.

blocks.heading: Story 1 — Intermittent stop on a filler (troubleshooting)
blocks.body: Situation: On Line 4 at fictional Northbridge Packaging, a filler stopped two or three times a shift with no repeatable alarm. Task: Maya owned finding a cause without blaming operators. Action: She logged timestamps, correlated with a flaky photoeye on a vibrating bracket, and added temporary monitoring before the permanent bracket fix. Result: Unplanned stops on that fault dropped to zero for the next month, and the work order included the vibration root cause — not just a swapped sensor.

blocks.heading: Story 1 in STAR bullets
rows: Filler stops 2–3×/shift, no clear alarm pattern
Find cause without guessing and without blaming people
Timestamp log → correlate → find vibrating photoeye bracket → monitor → permanent brace
Fault gone for a month; WO captured root cause

blocks.heading: Story 2 — Weekend PM that prevented a Monday failure (planning)
blocks.body: Situation: A gearbox on a case erector was due for oil analysis and showed rising wear metals. Task: Complete the PM inside a Saturday window without risking Monday's production start. Action: Maya staged seals and oil Friday, locked out Saturday morning, finished the change, and ran a dry cycle before releasing the line. Result: Monday started on time; the old oil report justified the work to the planner.

blocks.heading: Story 3 — Teaching a new tech LOTO (leadership / safety)
blocks.body: Situation: A new hire was about to open a panel that still showed bus voltage lamps lit. Task: Stop the unsafe step and turn it into training without humiliation. Action: Maya halted the work, walked the verify-zero-energy steps together, and added a checklist note the crew now uses. Result: Near miss documented; new hire completed supervised LOTO drills the same week.

blocks.heading: Backup angles if they dig deeper

columns.name: Safety culture
columns.detail: Use Story 3; emphasize verify, not assume.

columns.name: Documentation
columns.detail: Point at Story 1's work order that captured vibration, not only the part number.

columns.name: Teamwork
columns.detail: Add how Maya looped in the operator who first noticed the pattern — fictional partner 'Dee' on nights.

items.label: Speak each story out loud once under two minutes
items.detail: Cut adjectives; keep verbs and numbers.

items.label: Prepare one honest failure version
items.detail: What Maya would do differently on Story 1 if the bracket fix had been delayed.

items.label: Map stories to the job posting keywords
items.detail: Troubleshooting, PM discipline, safety — match their language without inventing skills.

items.label: Replace fiction with your facts before the real interview
items.detail: This page is a template, not a script to claim as your life.

blocks.heading: Practice prompt
blocks.prompt: An interviewer asks: "Tell me about a time you fixed a problem that kept coming back." Which prepared story fits best?
options: None — invent a new story on the spot
blocks.explanation: Recurring intermittent faults map to Story 1. Story 2 is planning/PM; Story 3 is safety coaching.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Match the question's shape: coming back = intermittent/chronic, which is Story 1.

blocks.heading: Your turn
blocks.body: Write three STAR cards from your real work this week. Keep Maya's structure; use your verified results.
